entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Aleksandr Mikhailovich Bakunin (d. December 18, 1854) was a prominent Russian diplomat, poet, and publicist whose life bridged the late 18th and mid-19th centuries, a period of profound social and intellectual ferment in the Russian Empire. As a scion of the Tver nobility and owner of the renowned Pryamukhino estate, Bakunin cultivated a vibrant intellectual salon that became a crucible for emerging Russian philosophical and literary movements. His significance lies not only in his own intellectual contributions but also as the patriarch of a family that profoundly impacted Russian thought, most notably through his revolutionary anarchist son, Mikhail Bakunin.

Bakunin's diplomatic career saw him serve in various capacities, including as Secretary of the Russian Embassy in Naples and later in Turin, providing him with exposure to European intellectual currents. Upon his return to Russia, he retired to his ancestral estate, Pryamukhino, in the Tver Governorate. Here, he transformed his home into a celebrated intellectual hub, frequently hosting luminaries such as the literary critic Vissarion Belinsky, the philosopher Nikolai Stankevich, and the historian Timofey Granovsky. These gatherings fostered critical discussions on German Idealism, French Enlightenment thought, and the future of Russia, significantly influencing a generation of Russian intelligentsia. His own literary output, though less celebrated than his social role, included poetry and publicist articles reflecting his engagement with contemporary philosophical debates.
